newsitem.title: TURKEY: Budget row looms for Turkey's Islamist PM.
newsitem.headline: Budget row looms for Turkey's Islamist PM.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist-led government, buoyed by its defeat of opposition attempts to force a confidence vote, on Thursday braced for a renewed attempt by its secularist rivals to bring it down in a protracted budget fight.

The government of Necmettin Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, survived a vote by 275 to 256 on Wednesday, heading off the no-confidence motion over his moves to turn his NATO-member country toward the Moslem world.
"We can see that support for the government in parliament has increased," Erbakan told reporters.
"The opposition is on the mat," crowed Erbakan's party daily, Milli Gazete, using a wrestling term.
Turkish investors, taking heart at any semblance of political stability, drove shares up 2.5 percent in morning trade to a midday record.
But economic and political problems still threaten Erbakan's shaky grip on power.

Chief among these is the 1997 budget battle, which main opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz has already vowed would be used to topple Erbakan's coalition partnership with the conservatives of the True Path Party (DYP).

"No one was expecting the government would be brought down by the censure motion, but yesterday's parliamentary debate signalled the difficulties awaiting the government in the budget discussions," wrote analyst Derya Sazak, in the daily Milliyet.
"It is understood that the second attempt at a (new) government will be made in the budget voting," Sazak said.
The government was to submit its budget plan to parliament later on Thursday, with final voting expected in late November.
However, it has been billed in advance as a "zero deficit" programme, something that opposition figures, as well as independent economists and bankers, say is unrealisitic.
Annual inflation is 80 percent and huge budget deficits have fed sky-high interest rates.
The Turkish lira has been sinking against the dollar each day. Foreign investors, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have demanded the government take decisive action.

Prospects for structural economic change, meanwhile, have not been helped by signs of discord between Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party and the free-marketeers of his DYP partners, in power for little more than 100 days.
An Erbakan proposal to index public sector wages to the dollar was quickly quashed by a DYP cabinet minister as out of the question.
The two parties have also clashed over Welfare's stated goals of eliminating domestic borrowing by the state -- a staple of Turkey's over-heated financial markets.
On the political front, things have not gone much better.
Erbakan has yet to carry out a promise to solve a 12-year-old Kurdish guerrilla conflict through "Moslem fellowship". More than 20,000 people have died in the fighting.
Disputes with neighbour Greece, over Cyprus and territorial rights in the Aegean Sea, are no nearer to a solution.
And his high-profile "Islamist" diplomacy, has alienated long-time patron the United States.

Turkey signed a gas accord with neighbour Iran during an Erbakan visit to Tehran, his first trip abroad as premier. The deal sailed close to a U.S. law banning new energy investment in Iran and Libya.
A later visit to Libya ended badly, after leader Muammar Gaddafi gave Erbakan a public dressing down over Turkey's treatment of its minority Kurds.
